docs.title: Home
docs.text:
SlingologyEIS reads the engine logs your Garmin avionics already record on every flight and answers two questions about each one:

  1. Did anything go outside the Rotax Operators Manual limits?
  2. Was this flight unusual for your engine?

The limits come from Rotax. The idea of "usual" comes from your own flight history. What to do about either is your call — the app never silences anything on its own, and it never stops watching something you've told it to tolerate.

Open SlingologyEIS — it runs entirely in your browser. There is nothing to install and no account; the analysis happens on your computer and the results stay there. Your logs stay in your own folders — the app reads them; it never copies or uploads them. If you would rather run it as a program on your own machine, you can (how).

Keep a copy of your workspace

Your workspaces are kept by your browser, on this device. Clearing the site's data removes them, and a browser short of space may clear them on its own. Settings → App → Export workspace… writes one file that restores everything — make one after your first analysis and whenever you have made decisions you would not want to redo. How.

No logs yet? Try the sample workspace

Download the sample workspace (10 MB) — a season of N117ZS, the Sling TSi the app was developed on: 19 flights, the three filters its owner set and why, and one annotation. Open the app, go to Settings → App → Import workspace… and pick the zip; the app analyses the flights in about a minute. Then look at Trends for the widening EGT spread, open the 2 September flight to see the fuel-pressure filter at work, and read the Journal. The sample is the same workspace the screenshots on this site were taken from.

Every flight in a workspace, with its insights at a glance.

docs.title: SlingologyEIS
docs.text: Engine health analytics for Rotax iS aircraft engines — built for how a FADEC engine actually works.

docs.title: Two ways to read this site
docs.text:
If you want to get going, start with the walkthroughs. They are picture-led and take you from opening the app to making your first decision about an insight:

  • Open the app and your first workspace
  • Reading your first flight
  • From an insight to a decision
  • Export and import

If you want to understand what the app is telling you, read the concept pages in order. Each one opens with a short In brief that tells you what the idea is and where you meet it in the app; the rest of the page explains how it works and which settings shape it. Stop whenever you have what you need.

  • Understanding your engine's data — what EIS tells you, why a FADEC engine is different, logs, flights and workspaces, phases of flight
  • What EIS watches — limits and events, your reference, topics and insights, the topics, cylinder balance
  • Deciding what matters — your decisions, Trends, the Journal
  • Working with others — sharing a workspace

docs.title: Found a problem? Have an idea?
docs.text: Tell us on the SlingologyEIS feedback board — no GitHub account needed. Report something that looks wrong, suggest a feature, or vote for the ideas other pilots have posted; the votes help decide what gets built next. When reporting a problem, say which page you were on, what you expected, what you saw and which browser you use; a screenshot helps. If the problem is in the analysis of a flight, a workspace export lets it be seen exactly as you see it — say in the report that you can share one.

docs.title: What this app is, and isn't
docs.text: SlingologyEIS is a reading aid for the data your engine already produces. It will show you when a reading went past a limit, when a flight looks different from your own history, and when something about your engine has been slowly changing. It will not tell you whether your aircraft is airworthy, and it does not replace the Operators Manual, your maintenance schedule or your mechanic. When the app says something is worth raising with your mechanic, that is what it means — a conversation starter with the evidence attached, not a diagnosis.

docs.title: Which engines
docs.text: Rotax 912iS, 915iS and 916iS. The Operators Manual limits for all three are built in and verified against the manuals. The analytics themselves were developed and validated on a 916iS; on the other engines each topic is marked unverified until there is data from such an aircraft. See The topics for the status of each.

docs.title: Which logs
docs.text:
Garmin G3X logs copied from the SD card, Garmin Pilot exports, and Garmin AXIS exports. The app recognises the format from the file itself, and a workspace can mix them.

Free and open source under the MIT licence. The project, its source code and the research paper behind the analytics are at github.com/AlchemyGeek/Rotax9iSEIS.

docs.title: Building the documentation site
docs.text:
The pilot documentation lives in this folder and is built with MkDocs and the Material theme.

pip install "mkdocs-material==9.7.*"
python3 docs/tools/gen_om_limits.py     # regenerate reference/om-limits.md from engines/*.json
mkdocs serve                             # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build --strict                    # static site into site/
mkdocs gh-deploy                         # publish to GitHub Pages

Layout:

  • concepts/ — one page per concept; In brief on top, how it works below, specs and paper as further reading
  • walkthroughs/ — picture-led, task-shaped pages
  • reference/ — limits (generated), settings, glossary, further reading
  • diagrams/ — hand-drawn SVGs inlined into concept pages (they follow the site's light/dark theme)
  • img/ — screenshots taken from the N117ZS workspace; retake as a batch after a UI change
  • specs/ and the research paper are kept here for developers and excluded from the site nav

docs.title: Theme override
docs.text: docs/overrides/partials/header.html is a copy of Material's header partial (from the version pinned in these instructions) with one addition: the Open the app button, which reads its address from extra.app_url in mkdocs.yml. After upgrading mkdocs-material, re-copy the partial from the new version and re-apply that block, or the header may miss newer theme changes.

docs.title: Starting the app
docs.text: SlingologyEIS runs in two ways. Both show the same screens and keep the same kind of workspace, and an export from one opens in the other.

docs.title: In your browser, from the website
docs.text:
1. Open https://alchemygeek.github.io/Rotax9iSEIS/app/ in Chrome or Safari on a Mac.
  2. The first visit downloads the analysis engine — about 30 MB, once. The page shows its progress.
  3. Create a workspace, then Choose folder… and pick the folder that holds your engine logs (or drop log files on the page). Sync analyses them.

Good to know:

  • Your logs stay on your computer. The engine runs inside the browser; nothing is uploaded. Workspaces are kept in the browser's private storage for this site.
  • It works offline after the first visit. Open the same address with no network and the app starts from your computer. When a new version is published, the next visit with a network switches to it and says Updated to version … once.
  • Safari asks for the folder again each visit. The folder shows Not connected — reconnect; pick it again, then Sync. Chrome remembers the folder and may ask you to Allow access with one click.
  • Keep a backup. The browser can clear a site's storage (for example when you clear browsing data). Settings → App → Export all workspaces… saves everything in one file you can import again.

docs.title: On your computer, as a local app
docs.text:
1. Install Python 3.10 or newer.
  2. Download the slingology_eis-….whl file from the latest release on GitHub and install it:
pip install slingology_eis-*.whl
  1. Start it, and open the address it prints (normally http://127.0.0.1:8420/):
slingology-eis serve

Your workspaces are kept in a SlingologyEIS folder in your home folder. Settings → App → Data location can move it. Add log folders by path; the app reads them where they are.

Stop the app with Ctrl-C in the terminal window.

docs.title: Publishing the website
docs.text:
Every push builds the site; CI keeps it as the artifact slingology-eis (slingology-eis-site.zip), and a release tag attaches it to the release. The site is plain files: it works from any folder of any static host, with no special server settings.

GitHub Pages serves this repository from the gh-pages branch, which the documentation already uses (mkdocs gh-deploy, at https://alchemygeek.github.io/Rotax9iSEIS/). The app goes in the app/ folder of the same site:

rm -rf docs/app && mkdir -p docs/app
unzip slingology-eis-site.zip -d docs/app      # from the release, or a CI run's artifact
mkdocs gh-deploy                               # publishes the docs with the app under app/

docs/app/ is not committed. Each publish adds the app's ~30 MB to the gh-pages branch history.

A custom domain is optional: set it in the repository's Settings → Pages. The app needs no change for it — the address in the first section changes, nothing else.

docs.title: Tagging a release
docs.text:
1. Set the version in pyproject.toml and slingology_eis/__init__.py (kept equal), and update CHANGELOG.md.
  2. Commit, then tag and push:
git tag v1.2.3
git push origin v1.2.3
  1. CI builds the tag, creates the GitHub release if there isn't one yet, and attaches the wheel and the site zip to it. Edit the release notes on GitHub if you want more than "See CHANGELOG.md."
  2. Publish the website from that release's site zip, as above.

docs.title: Cylinder balance
docs.text: In brief. On a FADEC engine the four cylinders should behave as a matched set, so the most telling single picture of engine health is how their cruise exhaust temperatures sit relative to one another — and whether that picture is changing. The app watches it two ways: the spread from hottest to coolest, and each cylinder's deviation from the other three. On Trends they are drawn together as one Cylinder balance panel: four lines that, on a healthy engine, run roughly flat and parallel.

docs.title: Why EGT pattern, not EGT level
docs.text:
The exhaust gas temperature of one cylinder on one flight depends on power, altitude, outside air and the day. The pattern across the four cylinders depends on the cylinders. Because the engine computer gives each cylinder the fuel and spark it intends, a cylinder that drifts away from its neighbours is telling you about an injector, a plug, an ignition coil or the probe itself — not about how the engine was leaned, because it wasn't.

Most engines have a cylinder that always runs hottest. On a turbocharged 915iS or 916iS it is usually cylinder 4, nearest the turbo exhaust. That is normal, and the app learns which cylinder is your usual hottest rather than assuming a flat ideal.

docs.title: Two measurements
docs.text:
Spread — hottest cruise EGT minus coolest — is the one-number summary, and the one the Operators Manual limits (392 °F between cylinders at normal fuel flow). The app compares each flight's spread with your usual spread in similar outside air temperature and watches for a widening trend over engine hours.

Deviation — each cylinder's cruise EGT minus the average of the other three — is the diagnostic version. It tells you which cylinder moved and in which direction. A cylinder running hotter than its own usual can mean a lean injector; cooler can point to ignition or a plug; erratic can point to the probe. The four deviations always sum to zero, so when one cylinder moves, the others appear to move the other way; the app reports the cylinder whose change is largest.

When one cylinder explains a widening spread, you get one insight under Cylinder EGT deviation, not two.

 engine hours °F vs others 0 Cyl 4 Cyl 3 Cyl 2 Cyl 1 usual pattern: flat, parallel · Cyl 4 hottest (turbo exhaust) Cyl 4 drifting away from the others → worth a look the four lines always sum to zero: when one moves up, the others appear to move down Healthy: four flat, parallel lines. Worth a look: one line drifting away.

docs.title: On the Flight view
docs.text: Two cards. Cylinder balance (EGT spread) gives this flight's spread, your usual, and the OM limit. Cylinder EGT deviation lists all four: Cyl 1 −33 °F (avg −32), Cyl 2 −18 °F (avg −9), Cyl 3 −4 °F (avg −7), Cyl 4 +55 °F (avg +48) — each cylinder against its own history. Both measure cruise only, so a flight without a settled cruise shows unavailable.

docs.title: On Trends
docs.text:
The Cylinder balance panel combines everything:

  • Four deviation lines over engine hours, with the reference band of whichever cylinder you select shaded behind them.
  • A hottest-cylinder strip: one mark per flight, shaped and coloured by which cylinder was hottest; hollow when its lead was under 15 °F (too close to call), ringed when it differed from your usual.
  • Usual hottest in the header — Cyl 4 (100 %, 57 flights, learned) — once one cylinder has won at least 70 % of ten or more flights by a clear margin. Until then the engine's expected cylinder is shown as a prior.
  • The spread strip below, with the OM limit drawn on it.

In the change summary at the top of Trends, the four deviations collapse to a single row naming the cylinder that moved most — cylinder 4 is about 5 °F running hotter than it used to (relative to the other cylinders) — and the spread ranks separately.

Trends → Cylinder balance: four deviation lines, the hottest-cylinder strip, and the spread.

docs.title: Reading it
docs.text:
• Four flat, parallel lines with the same cylinder hottest flight after flight: a healthy, consistent engine.
  • One line stepping or drifting away, especially if the hottest cylinder changes: look at that cylinder — injector, plug, coil, probe.
  • All four lines moving together cannot happen (they sum to zero); if the spread widens with no single cylinder responsible, the change is spread across cylinders and worth watching over more flights.
  • A noisy line on one cylinder with the others steady: probe or connector first.

As always, one flight is a note; a trend across flights is a conversation with your mechanic.

Further reading: Spec 08 (cylinder balance) and research paper §7.2 in the repository.

docs.title: Operators Manual limits and events
docs.text: In brief. The Rotax Operators Manual sets limits — temperatures, pressures, RPM, boost, time at takeoff power. When a reading crosses one for long enough to matter, the app records an event: when, in which phase, for how long and by how much. The engine computer's own ENGINE ECU alert is treated the same way, once the app has sorted the expected occurrences (start, lane check, shutdown) from the unexpected. Events are listed in the Events table on the Flight view and summarised on the Operators Manual limits card; a flight with any carries a LIMIT badge.

docs.title: Where the limits come from
docs.text:
Each workspace is tied to one engine model, and its limits come from that model's Operators Manual — the edition and revision are shown under Settings → Engine alongside the full table. The table is read-only: the limits are Rotax's, not the app's and not yours. What you control is what to do about an event that keeps happening (see Your decisions).

Twenty-one limits are checked on a 916iS, including per-cylinder EGT maximums, the EGT split between cylinders, manifold pressure, fuel pressure both ways, bus voltage both ways, and the five-minute rule for takeoff power. The 915iS and 912iS tables differ in a few values and in what exists at all — the 912iS has no turbo and no EGT-split limit. Operators Manual limits by engine lists them side by side.

Settings → Engine: every limit, its value, its severity label and when it is checked.

docs.title: How an event is found
docs.text:
A reading past a limit for a single second is not an event. Three rules keep the Events table honest:

Some limits need the excursion to last. Idle minimum must persist 30 s before it counts — a brief dip as the governor settles is normal. Fuel pressure minimum needs 10 s. Fuel pressure maximum needs 10 s in climb and descent but 30 s in cruise, where switching tanks causes a longer, harmless spike.

Some limits are only checked when they make sense. Low oil pressure, low fuel pressure and low voltage are not checked with the engine stopped. Oil pressure minimum is checked only once airborne. The oil-temperature-before-takeoff minimum is checked from the takeoff roll on. Fuel pressure maximum is not checked during taxi at all, because that is when you run the pump test. The Suppression column in the limits table shows these rules per limit.

Nearby excursions are one event. Once a reading has gone past a limit, the event does not end until the reading has been back inside for 30 s. A value that bounces across the line for two minutes is one two-minute event, not forty tiny ones.

What remains is listed in the Events table: time, phase, which limit, duration, how far past, and a link that jumps the chart to that moment. Each limit appears at most once per flight.

The Events table: one row per limit exceeded, with phase, duration and excess.

docs.title: Severity labels
docs.text: Each limit carries a label from the manual's own wording — WARNING or CAUTION — and each event inherits it. The labels are there to help you read the table. The app does not treat the two differently: it does not hide a caution, escalate a warning, or decide on your behalf that one deserves action and the other does not.

docs.title: Time at takeoff power
docs.text:
The manual allows takeoff power — above 5,500 rpm, or 100 % power — for no more than five minutes at a stretch. The app measures the longest continuous block you spent there (with the same 30 s rule joining brief dips). Going past 300 s is an event like any other. Coming within a minute of it is noted on the Time at takeoff power card as a close call, which usually means power was not reduced promptly after takeoff — a long climb-out, a delay — and is worth a glance at your habits rather than your engine.

The 5,800 rpm ceiling is separate: it is a hard limit with no time allowance. A brief overshoot as the governor catches a prop is the most common cause, and the kind of thing a filter with a small tolerance is for.

docs.title: Engine computer alerts
docs.text:
The engine computer raises an ENGINE ECU caution on the panel for many reasons, most of them routine. The app records every occurrence and sorts it by what the aircraft was doing:

When it happened What the app makes of it While the avionics and engine computer were coming up, before or during start Expected. Counted on the Engine computer alerts in flight card, nothing more. During the lane check — stationary, RPM in the lane-check band, two short runs Expected; this is the single-lane test. The flight header reports both lanes ✓, one lane only or not detected. At shutdown, as the engine is cut Expected. Counted only. On the ground with the engine running, but not a lane check An event. Listed in the Events table with the reason it is not a lane check — for instance that the RPM was below the lane-check band. In flight, from the takeoff roll to the landing roll An event, and the one that matters. Not expected; worth having the engine computer's fault log read at the next maintenance.

Occurrences shorter than a few seconds are counted as blips and not treated as events, because a single logged reading can be an artefact. The lane-check band depends on the engine — around 4,000 rpm on the 916iS and 912iS, around 2,500 rpm on the 915iS.

docs.title: Where events go next
docs.text:
Events are facts about one flight, but their pattern over many flights is what tells you about the engine. Every limit that has ever been exceeded in a workspace gets its own panel on the Trends page, showing on which flights it fired and by how much. And a limit that fires on every flight for a reason you understand — a sensor that reads a little high, an installation quirk — can be given a filter with a note, after which the app shows those events collapsed into one line and keeps watching for the day the pattern changes.

Further reading: Spec 01 (engine contract) §§ on limit detection and CAS classification, and Spec 09 (limit filters), in the repository.

docs.title: Logs, flights and workspaces
docs.text: In brief. A log is a file your avionics wrote. A flight is a log the app has decided actually left the ground. A workspace is the app's view of one aircraft: the folders its logs live in, plus everything the app has learned and every decision you have made. Your logs stay where they are — the app only reads them — and you can have as many workspaces as you like, one active at a time. You meet all three on the Flights page.

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
Your Garmin avionics record an engine log every time the system is powered up. The app reads three forms of it: a G3X log copied straight from the SD card (named like log_20261005_172050_KAWO.csv), a Garmin Pilot export of the same data (usually a long random file name), and a Garmin AXIS export. You do not need to tell the app which is which; it recognises the format from the file. A workspace can mix all three, and if you later swap a G3X for an AXIS, your engine-hours history carries straight on, because both record the same engine meter.

The app never copies, moves, renames or edits a log. It reads the file, remembers what it found, and keeps a fingerprint of the content so that if you rename or reorganise your folders later, Sync recognises the same log in its new place.

A fresh workspace: add the folder your logs live in, or drop files onto the page.

docs.title: Flights
docs.text:
Not every log is a flight. The avionics log an engine run with the aircraft never leaving the ground, a three-minute circuit, a session where the system was restarted halfway through. The app sorts these out when it first sees each log, and lists the ones it set aside under Skipped on the Flights page, each with its reason:

Reason What it means Ground session The aircraft never got airborne — an engine run, taxi or run-up only. Short flight Airborne for less than 10 minutes. Meant to catch pattern work too short to say anything about the engine; a twelve-minute hop still counts. Corrupt log A gap of more than five minutes inside one log, usually an avionics restart or an SD-card hiccup. Unreadable Not a Garmin engine log the app can read, or a file it could not analyse. The reason is shown; other logs are unaffected.

Two export paths for the same flight — the SD card copy and a Garmin Pilot export — are recognised as one flight and shown once, using the more complete file.

If you think the app got one wrong, open it: a skipped log opens read-only in a Log preview with its chart and alerts, and Include this log overrides the decision and analyses it. Nothing is ever deleted.

Skipped logs stay listed with their reason, and can be included.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
A workspace is where the app keeps everything it derives from your logs — each flight's analysis, your reference, the decisions you have made, your Journal. It is tied to one engine model, chosen when you create it, because the Operators Manual limits differ between the 912iS, 915iS and 916iS.

A workspace is defined by one or more log folders. Subfolders are included. Add the folder where you already keep your logs (Choose folder…, or drop files onto the page) and the app reads whatever is there; add logs to that folder and the next Sync picks them up. A single log that has gone missing keeps its results until you choose to remove it.

Because the app runs in your browser, it reads your folders only with the browser's permission. Chrome keeps that permission between visits and occasionally asks you to confirm it (Allow access on the folder row). Safari forgets it when you leave, so the row shows Not connected — reconnect on your next visit; everything already analysed is still there, and you reconnect only to sync new logs or open a flight's charts. When the app runs as a program on your own computer instead, folders are typed as paths and stay connected; if one is on a disk that is unplugged, the app says so and offers Locate folder when it is back.

You can have as many workspaces as you like, and switch between them from the name in the top bar. Two reasons to have more than one:

  • Another aircraft. Everything the app learns about "usual" is learned from one engine and never applied to another, so a second aircraft needs its own workspace. If logs from two tail numbers end up in one workspace the app notices and says so on every page where it matters.
  • An experiment. A workspace that points at a folder holding only some of your logs — one season, one engine-hours range — gives you the same analysis on just those flights. The app does not filter flights for you; you choose by organising files in folders.

The workspace name is yours. The one you were last using reopens when you start the app.

docs.title: Sync and re-analysis
docs.text: Sync rescans the workspace's folders, finds new and moved logs, and asks before analysing: Found N new logs. Analyze now? It also tells you when existing flights need re-analysis — after an update to the analysis itself, or after you change something that affects every flight, such as assigning a log channel. Say yes once and the Flights page shows per-flight progress.

docs.title: Where things are stored
docs.text:
What Where Your logs Wherever you keep them. Never copied or modified. (Logs that arrived inside an imported workspace are the one exception: the app keeps its own copy of those, with that workspace.) Workspaces and their results In your browser's private storage for the site — on this device, in this browser. Settings → App → Storage shows the space used and whether the browser has agreed to keep it; Delete all data there empties it. It survives restarts and app updates, but not clearing the site's data, so keep a workspace export as your backup. Derived from your logs; safe to delete and rebuild. …when you run the app on your own computer A data folder (~/SlingologyEIS by default, shown and changeable under Settings → App → Data location). Back it up like any other folder.

A workspace belongs to the browser it was made in. To use it in another browser or on another computer, export it there and import it here — the export carries every decision you made, and the logs if you ask.

Walkthrough: Open the app and your first workspace.

docs.title: Phases of flight
docs.text: In brief. The app splits every flight into phases — pre-start, engine start, warm-up, taxi, takeoff roll, climb, cruise, descent, approach, landing roll, shutdown — from the RPM, airspeed and altitude in the log, with nothing for you to label. Almost everything else depends on this: cylinder balance is measured in cruise, boost on the takeoff roll, and a reading that is expected to be out of range during the pump test or at shutdown is only known to be expected because the app knows the phase. You see the phases as coloured bands on the Flight view timeline.

docs.title: Why phases come first
docs.text:
Engine readings only mean something in context. 47 psi of fuel pressure is above the manual's maximum, and on a long cruise that is worth knowing; during the fuel-pump test on the taxiway it is what the test is for. 0 volts at the end of a log is the master switch going off, not an electrical failure. EGT spread during the climb says little; during a settled cruise it says a lot.

Without phase awareness the fuel-pressure maximum "fired" on four flights out of five and the low-voltage limit on half of them, which is the fastest way to teach a pilot to ignore every alert. So the first thing the app does with a log is work out, second by second, what the aircraft was doing.

 pre-start start warm-up taxi takeoff roll climb cruise descent approach landing shutdown time → Oil and coolant peaks · time at takeoff power · OM limits (phase-aware) Cylinder balance · cylinder deviation · cruise fuel facts Turbo boost at takeoff fuel pump test — fuel pressure max not checked lane check (ENGINE ECU expected) Which parts of a flight feed which topics.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text:
Phase What the app is seeing Pre start Avionics on, engine not running. Engine start RPM coming up from zero. Warm-up Engine running, aircraft stationary. Taxi Moving on the ground. A run-up that drops back to idle without leaving the ground stays in taxi. Takeoff roll High RPM, still below flying speed and close to the ground. Climb Flying and gaining height steadily. Cruise Flying with the altitude held for long enough to settle — about a minute. Descent Losing height steadily. Approach Low and slowing, near the end of the flight. Landing roll Back on the ground, slowing, RPM low. Shutdown Engine stopping.

Everything is read from the log's own channels — RPM, indicated airspeed, altitude, vertical speed — after a little smoothing so that a single noisy reading cannot flip a phase. Field elevation is taken from the altitude while stationary before takeoff, and re-read wherever the aircraft next touches down, so a flight that lands at a higher airfield than it left still ends correctly.

The caption under the timeline chart lists how long the flight spent in each phase: taxi 6m 0s · takeoff roll 14s · climb 1m 51s · cruise 7m 20s … Hover the chart and the phase at the cursor is named.

Phases as coloured bands under the traces, with their durations listed below.

docs.title: What uses which phase
docs.text:
• Cylinder balance and cylinder EGT deviation use cruise only, where the engine is settled and the four cylinders can be compared fairly.
  • Turbo boost at takeoff uses the takeoff roll, at full power.
  • Time at takeoff power counts every second above the takeoff-power threshold, whatever the phase.
  • Oil and coolant peaks look at the whole flight.
  • Several Operators Manual limits are checked only in certain phases — oil pressure minimum only once airborne, oil temperature before takeoff only from the takeoff roll on, fuel pressure maximum not at all during taxi (the pump test) and only after a longer excursion in cruise (tank switching). The full list, limit by limit, is under Settings → Engine.
  • Engine computer (ENGINE ECU) alerts are sorted by phase into expected (at start, during the lane check, at shutdown) and not expected (on the ground with the engine running, or in flight). See Operators Manual limits and events.

docs.title: When there is no cruise
docs.text: A short flight, a pattern session or a flight that never settled may have no cruise at all. The cruise-based cards then say unavailable: no cruise detected rather than reporting a number from a few seconds of level flight, and the chart carries a note that phase detection did not find a clear climb or cruise. The flight still counts for everything that does not need cruise.

docs.title: Settings that shape this
docs.text: There are none to adjust. Phase detection is deliberately automatic; it uses the same rules on every flight and every aircraft so that flights stay comparable.

docs.title: Sharing a workspace
docs.text: In brief. Settings → App → Export workspace… writes a file you can send to another pilot, your mechanic, or someone helping you read your engine. It carries your settings and decisions and — with Include logs — the logs themselves, so the recipient opens it and sees exactly what you see. Anonymise logs replaces the aircraft identity with a pseudonym and blanks the position and radio data. The recipient uses Import workspace… and gets a new workspace of their own.

docs.title: Why export a whole workspace
docs.text: The export is also how a workspace moves between browsers or computers, and your backup against the browser clearing its storage — the same file does all three. The useful thing to share is rarely one number. It is "look at this engine" — the flights, the way the limits have been tolerated, the trend that worried you. A workspace export carries all of that in one file, so the person at the other end sees your Flight views, your Trends and your Journal rather than a screenshot and a description.

docs.title: What the export contains
docs.text:
Always: the workspace's settings, its reference and model settings, which flights are excluded and why, pinned references, every filter and rule edit, the Journal, your annotations, and a list of the flights in it. Not carried: the analysis results themselves (the recipient's app recomputes them from the logs), your folder paths, or anything about your computer.

With Include logs (on by default): the log files, zipped together with the workspace. Without them the export is a small file that describes a workspace but cannot show one; the recipient sees Link your logs to see this workspace's analysis. Sharing with the logs is the normal case.

With Anonymise logs: the tail number and avionics system ID are replaced by a pseudonym (one per aircraft), GPS position and the nav/com columns are blanked, and the files are renamed flight_001.csv, flight_002.csv … Dates, times and engine hours are not changed — they are what makes the analysis work. Nor is anything you typed: your notes, filter reasons and the workspace name go as written, and the export dialog lists where your tail number appears in them so you can edit first.

To share only some flights, make a workspace that points at a folder with just those logs, and export that.

Settings → App: export with or without logs, anonymised or not, with the privacy note.

docs.title: What the recipient gets
docs.text:
Import workspace… (under Settings → App, or from the workspace switcher) always creates a new workspace, named after yours with (imported) added. It first shows a summary — whose it is, which engine, how many flights, how many filters and rule edits — then unpacks the logs into a folder of its own and matches them against your flight list: 38 of 40 flights found · 2 missing · 12 other logs held out. Then the usual analysis runs.

The recipient sees your workspace as you saw it: your filters, your exclusions, your pins, your Journal. A flight whose log did not arrive is listed under Skipped as In the sender's workspace — log not found, and your decisions about it wait until the log appears. A log that was in the zip but not in your workspace — perhaps you had skipped it — is held out, listed with Include if they want it.

An import from a newer version of the app than the recipient is running is refused with a message; from an older one it proceeds with a notice.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
An engine log carries more than engine data: your tail number, your avionics' serial number, the date and time of every flight, and your GPS track. Anonymising removes the identity and the track; it leaves the dates and times, because trends over engine hours need them. If that is more than you want to share, share fewer flights. The app shows this notice every time you export.

Walkthrough: Export and import.

docs.title: The Journal
docs.text: In brief. The Journal lists every decision currently in force in the workspace — each filter, rule edit, excluded flight, pinned reference, changed setting and annotation — with what it is doing right now. It is a register, not a log: reverse a decision and its entry disappears; edit one and its entry updates. Anything that needs your attention — a filter that has been breached or is drifting, a decision that no longer does anything — floats to the top, and the count on the Journal item in the top bar tells you how many.

docs.title: Why a register and not a history
docs.text:
A pilot managing an aircraft wants to know what is in effect. Which limits have I tolerated, and within what bounds? Which rules have I changed from the defaults? Which flights are out of the reference, and why? A history of every change ever made answers a different question, and buries the first one. So the Journal keeps one entry per live decision and nothing else. There is no settings changelog; if a setting differs from the app's default, the Journal lists it with both values.

Decisions in force, each with what it is doing now.

docs.title: What is listed
docs.text:
Kind Entry shows Filter The limit, its OM value, your band, duration and excluded phases, your note; the filter's status (Stable, Drifting, Breached, Review due, Quiet, Collecting); two small charts of how far past the limit and how long, with the filter's reference shaded and breaches ringed; actions to edit, re-baseline, mark reviewed or remove; Copy filters from… another workspace with the same engine. Rule edit The topic and trigger, the current value beside the shipped default. Disabled topic The topic, with Enable. Excluded from reference The flight and your reason, with Include again. Reference pinned The metric, the pinned flights and your label, with Unpin. Changed setting Any Reference & Models value that differs from the default, one entry per setting. Annotation A note you attached to a flight or event — the only thing the Journal creates itself. Acknowledged insight Reserved for single-insight acknowledgements, which are planned.

Every entry carries a link to the flight, limit, topic or metric it concerns, when it was made and last changed, and a live count of its effect, recomputed when you open the page: suppressing 9 events on 6 flights, currently suppresses nothing. Entries can be filtered by kind and grouped by date or by flight.

docs.title: Change notices
docs.text:
Some entries need you. They move to the top and are counted on the nav badge:

  • A filter that is breached or drifting (see Your decisions). The Flights page carries a one-line banner pointing here.
  • A decision with zero effect — a filter with nothing left to suppress, an exclusion that changes no verdict. Usually the cue to remove it.
  • A pinned reference older than the recent window — a reminder that the comparison is now against a fixed past.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: Changing the display units, the data location or updating the app creates no entry; none of those affects any result. And the Journal never contains anything the app decided on its own, because the app does not make decisions — it only records yours.

docs.title: The topics
docs.text:
In brief. Eight topics have a card on every Flight view. Each one below says what it measures, what it is compared against, when its insight fires and what the insight can point to. The text is the same as behind the ? on each card, with the Operators Manual values filled in for the 916iS; on a 915iS or 912iS the card shows that engine's values. The status line says on which engines the topic has been validated with real data.

Every topic was developed and validated on a Rotax 916iS. On the 915iS and 912iS the same analysis runs, but until logs from such an aircraft have confirmed it behaves sensibly there, the card carries Not yet validated on this engine. One topic does not exist on the 912iS at all, because the engine has no turbocharger.

Topic 916iS 915iS 912iS Cylinder balance (EGT spread) validated unverified unverified Cylinder EGT deviation validated unverified unverified Oil temperature peak validated unverified unverified Coolant temperature peak validated unverified unverified Time at takeoff power validated unverified unverified Turbo boost at takeoff validated unverified — Engine computer alerts in flight provisional unverified unverified Operators Manual limits validated unverified unverified

Provisional on the engine computer alerts means the sorting of alerts by phase has been checked against many flights, but no genuine in-flight alert has yet occurred in the data, so that case has not been seen for real.

docs.title: Cylinder balance (EGT spread)
docs.text:
Your engine computer sets the fuel and spark for each cylinder, so the four exhaust gas temperatures (EGTs) should keep a consistent pattern from flight to flight. This topic measures the spread between the hottest and the coolest cylinder in cruise. It compares that spread with your own past flights in similar outside air temperature, and with the Operators Manual limit of 392 °F (which applies when fuel flow is above 3 L/h, i.e. at any normal power setting). It also watches whether the spread is slowly growing as engine hours build up.

A widening spread can point to an injector, spark plug or ignition problem. A single unusual flight is worth noting; a spread that keeps growing over several flights is worth raising with your mechanic. When one cylinder on its own explains the change, it is reported under Cylinder EGT deviation instead, so you see it once.

Measured in: cruise. Compared with: your reference (same temperature band) and the OM split limit. Insight fires on: a flight outside your usual range, or a widening trend over engine hours. See Cylinder balance.

docs.title: Cylinder EGT deviation
docs.text:
Every engine has its own cylinder pattern, and on many one cylinder always runs hotter than the rest. Instead of judging cylinders against a generic ideal, this topic compares each cylinder's cruise EGT, measured against the average of the other three, with that same cylinder's own history. It flags a flight that is clearly outside the cylinder's usual range once there are at least 10 comparable flights, and a steady drift up or down as engine hours build up.

A cylinder running hotter than usual can mean a lean injector; one running cooler can point to ignition or a spark plug; erratic readings often point to the EGT probe itself. If the change also means a different cylinder is now the hottest, the message says so.

Measured in: cruise. Compared with: each cylinder's own reference (same temperature band). Insight fires on: a cylinder outside its usual range, or a trend in either direction.

docs.title: Oil temperature peak
docs.text:
This shows the highest oil temperature reached during the flight and compares it with your usual peak on flights in similar outside air temperature. Short flights often end before the engine is fully warm, so a lower peak after a short hop is normal.

A peak well above your usual can point to reduced oil cooling — less airflow through the oil cooler, a partial blockage, or a long climb on a hot day. A peak well below your usual on a full-length flight can mean the oil is not getting warm enough. If the oil went past the Operators Manual limit of 248 °F, that is reported once, under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge.

Measured over: the whole flight. Compared with: your reference (same temperature band). Insight fires on: a peak outside your usual range.

docs.title: Coolant temperature peak
docs.text:
The cylinder heads are liquid-cooled through the radiator, and this shows the highest coolant temperature reached during the flight, compared with your usual peak on flights in similar outside air temperature. Short flights often end before the engine is fully warm, so a lower peak after a short hop is normal.

A peak well above your usual can point to the cooling system: airflow through the radiator, coolant level, the pressure cap or the thermostat. A peak well below your usual on a full-length flight is less common and worth a look at the sensor. If the coolant went past the Operators Manual limit of 248 °F, that is reported once, under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge.

Measured over: the whole flight. Compared with: your reference (same temperature band). Insight fires on: a peak outside your usual range.

docs.title: Time at takeoff power
docs.text:
The Operators Manual allows takeoff power — above 5,500 rpm or 100 % power — for no more than 5 minutes at a time. This topic measures the longest continuous stretch you spent there on this flight. Going past the limit is reported under Operators Manual limits, and this card shows the same badge. Coming within 60 seconds of it is noted as a close call: it often means power was not reduced promptly after takeoff, for example during a long climb-out or a delay. Reducing to climb power once you are safely airborne keeps you well clear.

Measured over: every second above the takeoff-power threshold. Compared with: the OM limit only. Insight fires on: the limit event, or a close call.

docs.title: Turbo boost at takeoff
docs.text:
915iS and 916iS only. At full takeoff power the turbocharger should deliver a manifold pressure (MAP) that depends mainly on airport elevation and outside air temperature. This topic learns that relationship from your own takeoffs and compares each takeoff's MAP with what your engine normally makes in the same conditions. A takeoff is flagged when the difference is larger than your takeoffs normally vary — about 2 times the usual scatter of your own data.

Lower than expected can point to the turbo, the wastegate or an intake leak; higher than expected is usually worth a sensor check. If a takeoff's elevation or temperature is outside anything your takeoffs have covered so far, the card says so instead of guessing.

Measured in: the takeoff roll, at full power. Compared with: your own boost model (needs 5 takeoffs). Insight fires on: a takeoff further from the model than your takeoffs normally scatter.

docs.title: Engine computer alerts in flight
docs.text:
The ENGINE ECU caution comes from the engine computer, and when it appears matters more than that it appears. This card sorts each occurrence by the flight phase it happens in and counts them: at start, while the avionics and the engine computer come up; during the lane check, when each lane is tested on its own; and at shutdown. Those are expected and are only counted here.

An occurrence on the ground with the engine running that is not a lane check, or one in flight from the takeoff roll to the landing roll, appears in the Events table with the other events of the flight, together with the reason it is not a lane check when it nearly is one, and you can filter or annotate it there like any limit event. An occurrence in flight is not expected, and it is worth having the engine computer's fault log read at the next maintenance. The card also says whether the lane check covered both lanes: both lanes ✓, one lane only (the log cannot identify the lane), or not detected. Occurrences shorter than 3 seconds are counted separately and not treated as events, since a single reading can be a logging artefact.

Measured over: the whole log, including the ground. Compared with: the expected pattern. Insight fires: never from this card — the unexpected occurrences are events on the limits card.

docs.title: Operators Manual limits
docs.text:
This checks every reading the engine reports against the limits in the Rotax Operators Manual for your engine: temperatures, pressures, RPM, manifold pressure, voltage, EGT split and time at takeoff power. Moments when a reading is expected to be out of range, such as engine start, warm-up or the fuel pump test, are allowed for, and very brief blips are ignored. Each limit that was exceeded appears once, with how long and by how much, and links to that moment on the chart. If a limit is exceeded on every flight because of a known sensor or installation characteristic, you can set a filter with a note; the app keeps watching the filtered limit and tells you if the pattern changes.

Compared with: the OM, with phase awareness. Insight fires on: any event. See Operators Manual limits and events.

docs.title: Flight facts
docs.text: Not a topic, but shown in the Flight view header: fuel burned, cruise miles per gallon, average cruise fuel flow and the lane check result. They are shown for planning, not as engine-health checks. They mostly reflect wind, weight and the power setting you chose rather than the engine itself: miles per gallon uses ground speed, so a headwind lowers it, and fuel flow is an estimate calculated by the engine computer, not a measurement. That is why these numbers never raise an alert.

docs.title: Topics you will not see
docs.text: Two things the app once tried are deliberately not topics. Climb thermal rate — how fast oil and coolant warm during the climb — turned out to vary more flight to flight than any change it could detect, so it is computed for research only and has no card. Cruise efficiency and cruise fuel flow were topics for a while and are now flight facts, for the reasons above. The app also never tries to detect ECO/POWER mode, because the throttle position that governs it is not in the log.

docs.title: Topics and insights
docs.text: In brief. A topic is one thing the app watches — oil temperature peak, cylinder balance, boost at takeoff. Each topic has a card on the Flight view. The card always carries an analysis line (this flight's number, your usual, the manual's limit), and sometimes an insight — a short statement that something about this flight is worth your attention. Cards with nothing to add stay collapsed to their one line. The flight's insights are gathered in the left column of the Flight view, and the Flights page shows each flight's count.

docs.title: The two-layer card
docs.text:
Every topic card is written in the same two layers so that you always know what you are looking at.

The analysis line is always present and purely descriptive. It states the measurement, your reference, and the limit, in one sentence:

Peak 183°F. Your average: 201°F ± 12°F (47 flights). OM limit: 248°F.

Nothing in it is a judgement. If this is all the card says, the flight was ordinary on that topic.

The insight appears only when one of the topic's triggers has fired — the flight sits outside your usual range, a trend has become clear, a limit was crossed. It says what was found in plain language and, where the app can say so without guessing, what it can point to: a widening cylinder spread can point to an injector or a plug; a boost lower than expected to the turbo, wastegate or an intake leak. The card expands, shows the insight with a severity label, and offers the actions that apply.

 Oil temperature peak Peak 183°F · Your avg 201 ± 12°F (47 flights) · OM 248°F Ordinary flight on this topic: the card stays on its one line. Cylinder balance (EGT spread) Spread 84°F · Your avg 61 ± 6°F (47 flights) · OM 392°F WATCH Wider than your usual on mild days: 84°F vs 61 ± 6°F. A widening spread can point to an injector, plug or ignition. View evidence → Exclude from reference → Edit trigger ↓ Analysis line always present · descriptive Insight only when a trigger fires · judgement Every card has the first line. Only some have the second.

Topic cards: collapsed to their analysis line unless there is something to say.

docs.title: What fires an insight
docs.text:
Each topic has one or more triggers, shown under the card's triggers disclosure with their current values and whether they were met:

Trigger Fires when Baseline deviation This flight sits outside your usual range for the metric (more than the outlier threshold, default 2 standard deviations), with at least n_min (default 10) comparable flights behind the comparison. Trend The metric has been moving steadily with engine hours — a straight line fits well enough (R² ≥ 0.5) over at least 10 flights, in the direction the topic cares about (cylinder spread only matters if it is widening; a cylinder's deviation matters either way). Threshold A fixed test: a limit was exceeded, or a takeoff's boost sat further from your own model than your takeoffs normally vary.

The triggers disclosure: each trigger, its values, and how close it came on this flight.

The card's triggers line shows how close a trigger came: trend · R² ≥ 0.5 · n ≥ 10 — not met: R² 0.30 over 23 flights. You can change the numbers for any topic from its card — see Your decisions — and the edit applies to every flight in the workspace.

docs.title: Severity labels
docs.text: Insights carry a label: LIMIT (an Operators Manual limit was crossed), WARNING, WATCH or INFO. As with events, the labels are a reading aid. The app does not hide an info, escalate a warning, or treat any of them as a verdict. What differs is only the colour on the Flights page, which shows each flight's worst label and count.

docs.title: One event, one card
docs.text: Where a topic concerns something that is also an Operators Manual limit — oil temperature peak and the oil maximum, coolant peak and the coolant maximum, time at takeoff power and the five-minute rule — the limit event is reported once, on the Operators Manual limits card and in the Events table, and the topic card simply mirrors the badge. You will not see the same exceedance raised twice in different words. Likewise, when one cylinder on its own explains a widening spread, the insight appears under Cylinder EGT deviation and the spread card points there.

docs.title: Still building, not yet validated
docs.text:
Two notes appear on cards and mean different things:

  • Still building your reference — N more flights means the comparison is not being made yet because there is not enough history. The number is shown; the judgement is withheld.
  • Not yet validated on this engine means the topic was developed and checked on a 916iS and no data from a 915iS or 912iS has yet confirmed that it behaves sensibly there. The card works; treat its insights with that in mind. The topics lists each topic's status by engine.

docs.title: What is not a topic
docs.text:
Fuel burned, cruise miles per gallon and cruise fuel flow appear in the Flight view header as flight facts — logbook figures for your planning. They mostly reflect wind, weight and the power you chose, miles per gallon uses ground speed, and fuel flow is the engine computer's estimate rather than a measurement. So they are shown but never compared and never raise an insight.

Walkthrough: Reading your first flight.

docs.title: Trends: is my engine changing?
docs.text: In brief. The Flight view asks whether one flight was unusual. Trends asks whether your engine has been changing: it compares your most recent flights — the last 10 engine hours or so — with everything before, metric by metric, and lists at the top the ones that have moved. Below the summary, one panel per area shows each metric over engine hours with your usual range shaded, the recent window marked, and the Operators Manual limit drawn where there is one. A number on the Trends item in the top bar tells you how many changes are open.

docs.title: Two different questions
docs.text:
A single unusual flight can be weather, a long taxi, a short hop. A metric that has shifted — whose recent average sits somewhere different from where it used to — is a change in the engine or its installation, and it can be small enough that no single flight was ever flagged. Trends is built to find the second kind.

 engine hours metric reference: earlier flights, average ± 1σ recent window last 10 h · 5–15 flights recent average shift no single recent flight is an outlier — but together they have moved Shift: the recent window's average sits away from the reference's average.

docs.title: The change summary
docs.text:
The top of the page is a plain-language list, one row per metric that has moved, ranked by how far it moved:

Cylinder balance · cylinder 4 — cylinder 4 is about 5.4 °F running hotter than it used to (relative to the other cylinders) — last 12 flights (10.3 h) vs. 46 earlier flights — and the rate of change has shifted

Each row names the area and metric, states the change in the metric's own units and direction, says which flights were compared, and adds qualifiers where they apply: the rate of change has shifted (a bend — the metric was drifting slowly and now drifts faster, or has started to); the recent average is within 25 % of the OM limit; it has reached the edge of your filter band; or, for a pinned reference, since . There are no severity colours here; the ranking is the message.

Under the list: N other metrics checked, no change. A collapsed Past changes section lists shifts that have since cleared.

The change summary: what has moved, by how much, compared with what.

docs.title: What "shift" means
docs.text:
For each metric the app takes the recent window — the newest flights spanning at least the last 10 engine hours, with at least 5 flights and at most 15 — and compares their average with the average of all your earlier contributing flights, using the same unusual threshold as everywhere else (2 standard errors by default). Where a metric depends on weather, recent flights are compared with earlier flights in the same temperature or density-altitude band when there are enough of them; otherwise the row says mixed comparison. A shift is also declared if the recent average has crossed the line at 75 % of the headroom to an Operators Manual limit, or the edge of a filter band, even if the move is statistically small.

The window is a setting, not a slider on the page: Settings → Reference & Models → Window.

docs.title: Rolling or pinned reference
docs.text:
By default the reference a metric is compared against is rolling — every earlier contributing flight, growing as you fly. That is right for watching a gradual drift.

Sometimes you want a fixed point: the twenty flights before you changed an injector, or before the annual. Pin reference to these flights on any panel fixes that metric's reference to the flights currently in the window and labels it; from then on every flight is compared with that set until you Unpin. The strip shows the pinned region hard-edged and marks later flights as not used for the reference. A pin is a decision, listed in the Journal, and the Journal will tell you when a pin is older than the recent window. Filters keep their own frozen reference regardless of pins.

docs.title: The panels
docs.text:
Below the summary, metrics are grouped into panels. Each strip plots the metric against engine hours, one point per flight, with your usual range (mean ± 1σ) shaded, the recent window highlighted, outliers ringed, and the OM limit drawn as a labelled line where one exists, with a fainter line at 75 % of the headroom. Click a point to open that flight. Stratify by OAT/DA redraws the band per weather condition. Show detail strips adds the whole-history fit and time-above-limit.

  • Cylinder balance — the four deviation lines, the hottest-cylinder strip, and the spread. See Cylinder balance.
  • Thermal — oil and coolant peaks, with climb thermal rate as context.
  • Boost / power — time at takeoff power against the 300 s limit; boost at takeoff as the difference from your own model (the model's fit is in the caption).
  • Fuel · planning — cruise efficiency and cruise fuel flow. Marked planning because they reflect wind, weight and power setting; listed last.
  • Limit: … — one panel per Operators Manual limit that is filtered or has ever been exceeded in this workspace. The first strip is an event strip: a tick per flight that had an event, headed exceeded on 2 of 12 recent flights · 1 of 46 earlier — how often is the primary signal. Below it, the size of the excess on the flights that had one, with the limit as the zero line and any filter band drawn.
  • Alert: ENGINE ECU — the same event strip for engine-computer alerts that were not expected.
  • Never exceeded (N) — a collapsed group of limits with nothing to show.

One strip: reference band, recent window, outliers ringed, the OM limit drawn.

docs.title: Readiness notes
docs.text: A strip that cannot yet say anything says why: building reference · N more flights, too few flights, conditions not comparable yet, never exceeded, filtered, baseline pinned. These are the same situations as on the Flight view cards; the Trends page simply shows them per metric.

docs.title: Settings that shape this
docs.text: Setting Default Where Recent window (hours) 10 h Settings → Reference & Models → Window Min / max flights in window 5 / 15 same OM margin fraction 0.25 (the 75 % line) same Outlier z-threshold 2.0 Settings → Reference & Models → Comparison Pinned references none per panel on Trends; listed under Reference & Models

docs.title: What Trends does not do yet
docs.text:
Projecting when a drifting metric would reach its limit, marking maintenance events on the time axis, and a strip of operating conditions under each chart are planned for a later version.

Further reading: Spec 12 (Trends as a change page) in the repository.

docs.title: What EIS tells you
docs.text: In brief. Every flight is checked in two independent ways. First against the Rotax Operators Manual — fixed limits that apply to every engine of your model. Second against your own history — what this particular engine usually does in similar conditions. The first produces events; the second produces insights. Both appear on the Flight view, and the long-term version of the second is the Trends page.

docs.title: Two questions, two kinds of answer
docs.text:
Engine monitoring tools usually blur two different questions together. SlingologyEIS keeps them apart because they call for different responses.

Did anything go past a limit? The Operators Manual gives numbers — maximum oil temperature, minimum fuel pressure, how long you may stay at takeoff power. These are the same for every 916iS, or every 915iS, or every 912iS. When a reading crosses one of them for long enough to matter, the app records an event: when it happened, in which phase of flight, for how long, and by how much. Events are facts about the flight. They are listed in the Events table on the Flight view, and a flight that had any carries a LIMIT badge on the Flights page.

Was this flight unusual for my engine? No manual can tell you what your oil temperature peak normally is on a mild day, or how far apart your four cylinders' exhaust temperatures usually sit. The app learns that from your previous flights and calls it your reference. Each flight is then compared with the reference, metric by metric. When something sits clearly outside its usual range — or has been drifting steadily as engine hours build — the app raises an insight. Insights are judgements, not facts, and they are only as good as the history behind them, which is why the first ten or so flights say still building.

 One flight every reading, every second checked against Operators Manual limits the same for every engine of your model produces Events facts: when, how long, how far compared with Your reference learned from your own flights produces Insights judgements: unusual for you? Limits are the same for every engine of your model. The reference is yours alone.

docs.title: Where you meet it
docs.text:
On the Flight view, the left column lists the flight's insights and the header shows its flight facts — fuel burned, cruise miles per gallon — which are just numbers for your planning and never raise an alert. Below the timeline chart sits the Events table (limits and alerts), and below that the Analysis section with one card per topic. A card with nothing to say is collapsed to a single line: Peak 183°F. Your average: 201°F ± 12°F (47 flights). OM limit: 248°F. That line always shows the three things side by side — this flight, your usual, and the manual's limit.

The Flight view: this flight's insights, flight facts, the timeline with its phases, and the events table.

The Trends page asks the second question over a longer horizon: not "is this flight unusual" but "has my engine been changing". See Trends.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The two checks run on every flight the moment it is analysed, and again whenever something that affects them changes — a new engine version, a rule you edited, a flight you excluded from the reference.

The limit check reads every value the engine reported against the limit table for your engine model (you can see the whole table under Settings → Engine). It knows about the moments when a reading is expected to be out of range — the fuel pump test before takeoff, a cold start, idle on the ground — and allows for them, so you are not told about things that are part of normal operation. Brief single-reading blips are ignored. What remains becomes events. Operators Manual limits and events explains the details.

The reference check takes each metric the app tracks — about thirty of them — and asks how this flight's value compares with the same metric on your earlier flights, preferably flights flown in similar outside air temperature or density altitude. "Clearly outside the usual range" means more than about two standard deviations from your average; that threshold is the outlier z-threshold in Settings → Reference & Models (default 2.0). Your reference explains how the reference is built and why it is never shared between aircraft.

docs.title: What the app does not do
docs.text:
It does not grade the flight, score the engine or combine the two questions into a single verdict. It does not decide for you that an event you have seen a hundred times is fine — but it gives you a way to say so yourself, with a note, and then keeps watching for the day that event changes. See Your decisions.

Further reading: the research paper Rotax 91XiS Engine Data Analytics sets out the reasoning behind this two-question design.

docs.title: Why a FADEC Rotax is different
docs.text: In brief. On a Rotax iS engine the engine computer — not you — sets the fuel and the spark. Most engine-analysis tools were built for engines where the pilot leans the mixture by hand, and their signature diagnostics (rich-of-peak, lean-of-peak, mixture sweeps) have no meaning here. SlingologyEIS starts from what the iS engine actually controls and what its log actually contains, which is why its topics look different from what you may have seen elsewhere.

docs.title: What the engine computer does
docs.text:
The 912iS, 915iS and 916iS are full-authority engines: a dual-redundant engine control unit (two lanes, A and B) reads throttle position, air temperature, manifold pressure and the rest, and from them decides injector timing, ignition advance and — above roughly 97 % throttle — whether the engine runs in ECO or POWER mode. There is no mixture lever and no magneto switch. The pilot has one input, the throttle, and the computer does the rest.

That is good news for engine health: the mixture is always what the computer intends, so a cylinder running hot or cool is telling you about that cylinder — its injector, plug, probe or airflow — not about how the engine was leaned. It also means the pilot-centred diagnostics of other tools do not apply.

docs.title: What other tools assume
docs.text:
Platforms such as Savvy Aviation and FlySto grew up around Lycoming and Continental engines, where the central engine-management question is how the pilot handles the mixture. Their signature analyses — finding peak EGT during a lean sweep, judging rich-of-peak versus lean-of-peak operation, spotting an exhaust valve from the EGT pattern during leaning — depend on the mixture being varied by hand. On a FADEC engine the mixture is never varied by hand, so those analyses either cannot run or produce noise. FlySto will replay your flight and graph any channel, which is useful, but it has no engine-health model for an iS engine. Rotax's own diagnostic software reads the engine computer's fault log directly, but it needs a hardware interface and is used at maintenance, not after every flight.

So a pilot with a Rotax iS engine and a modern glass panel has been collecting a rich engine log every flight with nothing designed to read it. That is the gap this app fills.

docs.title: What is, and is not, in the log
docs.text:
Everything the app knows comes from the engine log your Garmin avionics write — G3X, Garmin Pilot export or AXIS. That log carries RPM, manifold pressure, oil temperature and pressure, coolant temperature, four exhaust gas temperatures, fuel pressure and flow, bus voltage, the CAS alerts, and the flight data (airspeed, altitude, position, outside air temperature) that the app needs to work out what phase of flight you were in.

Some things the engine computer knows never reach the log: throttle position, which lane is active, injector pulse width, ignition advance, wastegate position. The app does not try to guess them. Two consequences matter to how you read its output:

  • Fuel flow is an estimate. The Rotax iS reports a fuel flow calculated by the engine computer from injector timing, not measured by a sensor, and Rotax quotes a tolerance of about ±10 %. That is why fuel burned and miles per gallon appear as flight facts for your planning and never raise an alert.
  • The cooling system is split. The cylinder heads are liquid-cooled and the barrels air-cooled, so the health signals are coolant temperature and EGT, not cylinder-head temperature as on an air-cooled engine. The app's thermal topics follow that split.

docs.title: How this shapes the topics
docs.text:
With the mixture fixed by the computer, the useful questions become:

  • Are the four cylinders behaving as a matched set, and is the one that runs hottest the one that usually does? → Cylinder balance
  • Are the oil and coolant peaks what they usually are for this weather? → oil and coolant peak topics
  • Is the turbocharger delivering the boost it usually does for this elevation and temperature? → Turbo boost at takeoff (915iS and 916iS)
  • Did you stay within the time the manual allows at takeoff power? → Time at takeoff power
  • Did the engine computer raise an alert at a moment when it shouldn't? → Engine computer alerts in flight

And underneath all of them, the Operators Manual limits, checked with an understanding of when a reading is expected to be out of range. See The topics for the full list and Operators Manual limits and events for how limits are checked.

Further reading: the research paper Rotax 91XiS Engine Data Analytics, sections 1–2, sets out this argument in full with references to the Rotax documentation.

docs.title: Your decisions
docs.text: In brief. The app reports; you decide. When an event or an insight is something you understand and accept, you can tell the app so — with a filter on a limit, an edit to a topic's rules, a flight excluded from the reference, or a disabled topic. Each decision says plainly whether it applies to this flight only or to all flights in this workspace, and shows you its effect before you confirm. Every decision in force is listed in the Journal, and the app keeps watching the thing you tolerated and tells you when it changes.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Every engine has quirks. A fuel-pressure sender that reads a couple of psi high. A prop governor that lets the RPM touch 5,820 for a few seconds on every takeoff. A cylinder that has always run 50 °F hotter. Report them once and they are information; report them on every flight and they are noise that buries the thing you actually need to see.

The app will not decide for you that a quirk is harmless. What it offers instead is a way for you to say so, in a form that is recorded, reversible, and still watched. That last part matters: a filtered limit is not switched off. The app keeps measuring it and tells you if the pattern changes — if the sender starts reading five psi high instead of two, or the overshoot starts lasting longer.

docs.title: Scope: this flight, or every flight?
docs.text:
The question to ask of any decision is what does it apply to. The app answers it on every control before you confirm, with a caption such as All flights in this workspace — this limit or This flight only. The distinction:

  • A filter or a rule edit is a statement about your engine. It applies to every flight, past and future, in the workspace. Editing a trigger from one flight's card does not make the edit about that flight.
  • Excluding a flight from the reference is a statement about one flight. It applies to that flight only — though because the reference is built from all the others, other flights' comparisons will move a little.
 This flight only a statement about one flight • Exclude from the reference (with a reason) • Annotate an event or the flight • Acknowledge one insight (planned) All flights in this workspace a statement about your engine · past and future flights • Filter a limit (magnitude · duration · phases) • Edit a topic's triggers · disable a topic • Pin a metric's reference Journal every decision in force live effect reversible listed A filtered limit stays watched: the app reports when the pattern changes. Most decisions are about the engine, and so about every flight.

docs.title: Filter a limit
docs.text:
A filter says: on my aircraft this limit is exceeded in a way I understand and accept, within these bounds. One filter per limit per workspace, created from any event row (Filter this limit…) or from the limit's insight card. It has up to three independent conditions, and an event is tolerated if any one of them covers it:

  • Magnitude — "a little past the limit is fine": up to a fixed amount in the limit's own units (say +2.5 psi), a percentage of the limit, or, once there is enough history, a number of standard deviations from the filter's own reference.
  • Duration — "brief excursions are fine": events up to N seconds are tolerated.
  • Excluded phases — "not during taxi": an event lying wholly within the phases you tick is tolerated. The app can pre-select the phase of the event you started from, but only if you ask.

Before you save, a preview says exactly what the filter would do across the workspace: This would hide 412 events on 38 flights; 2 flights would still show a breach. A note is required for a WARNING limit and optional for a CAUTION; one limit — oil pressure minimum — can never be filtered, and the 5,800 rpm ceiling allows only a small absolute tolerance.

Afterwards, tolerated events collapse on every Flight view into one line per limit — 17 fuel pressure events within your filter, up to +2.5 psi — expandable if you want the detail. An event the filter does not cover is a breach: shown as an ordinary row, marked beyond your filter.

Creating a filter: the conditions, the note, and what it would do across the workspace.

The filter's card in the Journal: its status, every flight's excess against the band, and the reference it watches against.

What the app keeps watching. When you create a filter it freezes a reference — your twenty most recent flights that had this event — and from then on compares every new flight with it. The filter's card in the Journal reports a status: Stable; Breached (an event the filter did not cover); Drifting (the last couple of flights went further past the limit, or events are becoming more frequent, than the reference); Review due (a set number of engine hours has passed); Quiet (no events on the last ten flights — perhaps the filter is no longer needed). Breached and drifting filters are counted on the Journal badge and announced in a banner on the Flights page. Mark reviewed clears a breach or a review; drift clears itself when the pattern settles, or you Re-baseline the filter if the new pattern is the one you now accept.

docs.title: Edit a topic's rules
docs.text:
Every topic card shows its triggers and their current values under ▸ triggers. Edit rules… (or Edit trigger ↓ on an insight) opens an editor beside the card where you can change the numbers — how many flights a comparison needs, how strong a trend must be before it is reported, a trigger's severity label — or switch the topic off. Triggers that follow an Operators Manual limit are shown as such and cannot be given a different number.

As you edit, a live preview counts the effect across the workspace: On your 58 flights: 4 changes (1 newly flagged, 3 cleared), with the affected flights linked. Apply to all flights saves it; Reset to shipped puts a rule back to the app's default. While any rule differs from shipped, the Journal shows the current and shipped values side by side.

Editing a trigger: the values, and what would change across every flight.

docs.title: Disable a topic
docs.text: The enabled switch in the same editor. The card stays on every Flight view, collapsed to one line — Cylinder balance · disabled · Enable — so you can always see that a topic is off and turn it back on in context. Disabling Operators Manual limits hides that card's insights only; events are still detected, still feed filters, and still appear on Trends.

docs.title: Exclude a flight from the reference
docs.text: From the flight's header, the In reference mark on the Flights page, or an insight's Exclude this flight from reference →. You give a reason — a post-maintenance test flight, a known bad probe, a ferry flight flown unlike your norm — and the flight stops shaping what other flights are compared against. It keeps its own analysis and its own insights. The change takes effect on the next Rebuild reference (Settings → Reference & Models), and the preview tells you whether any flight's verdict would change. Include again reverses it through the same dialog.

docs.title: Pin a metric's reference
docs.text: On the Trends page, Pin reference to these flights fixes a metric's baseline to a chosen set of flights instead of the rolling history. It is a decision like the others — recorded in the Journal, reversible with Unpin — and is described on the Trends page.

docs.title: Acknowledge a single insight
docs.text:
Sometimes an insight is right, you have looked, and there is nothing more to do — a hot day, a known short flight. Acknowledging it is a this flight only decision that marks that one insight as seen without changing any rule. The Journal has a place for these.

Note

Acknowledging from the insight card is planned and not yet in the app. Until it arrives, the way to note "seen, no action" on one flight is an annotation on the event or flight.

docs.title: Undoing
docs.text:
Every decision is listed in the Journal with its current effect and an edit or remove action. Removing a filter, resetting a rule, re-including a flight or unpinning a reference deletes the Journal entry; nothing is kept as history. If a decision is currently doing nothing — a filter with no events to suppress, an exclusion that changes no verdict — the Journal says so, which is usually the cue to remove it.

Walkthrough: From an insight to a decision. Further reading: Spec 09 (limit filters) and Spec 14 (settings, Journal and rule editing) in the repository.

docs.title: Your reference
docs.text: In brief. Your reference is what the app has learned, from your own flights, about what each reading usually is on this engine — the average and the normal scatter, ideally on days with similar weather. Every flight is compared with it, and a reading well outside its usual range becomes an insight. It takes about ten flights to form; until then cards say still building. It is learned from one aircraft and never applied to another. You see it in every card's Your average: … ± … (N flights) line, as the shaded band on Trends charts, and under Settings → Reference & Models.

docs.title: Why "usual" has to be yours
docs.text: Two 916iS engines in two Sling TSis will not run the same oil temperature on the same day. Cowling, baffling, oil cooler, probe placement, the individual engine — all of it shifts the numbers by more than the differences the app is trying to detect. A fleet-wide "normal" would hide exactly the changes that matter. So the app builds its idea of normal from your flights alone, and when it says higher than usual it means higher than your usual. The only numbers shared between aircraft are the Operators Manual limits.

docs.title: How the reference is built
docs.text:
