docs.title: Settings and their defaults
docs.text: Everything you can change, where it lives, its shipped default, and what changing it does. Each entry is the same sentence shown behind the ⓘ in the app. Settings marked workspace apply to every flight in the active workspace; those marked app apply to every workspace.

docs.title: Settings → Reference & Models
docs.text: Setting Default Scope What it does Contributing flights all admitted flights workspace The flights that define what normal looks like for your engine — every other flight is judged against them. Exclude a flight from its header or an insight; Rebuild reference applies the change. Outlier z-threshold 2.0 workspace How far from your usual a flight must be before it is called out — lower flags more flights, including more ordinary variation. n_min (per trigger) 10 workspace How many of your other flights are needed before this check runs — lower starts checking sooner, against a less settled picture of normal. Shown here; edited on each topic's card. Recent window (hours) 10 h workspace How many of your latest flights Trends checks against the reference — a smaller window shows a change sooner but can be swayed by one odd flight. Min / max flights in window 5 / 15 workspace The window always holds at least the minimum and never more than the maximum, whatever the hours say. OM margin fraction 0.25 workspace Where Trends draws the headroom line: 0.25 means a shift is declared when the recent average has used 75 % of the way to an Operators Manual limit. Reference per metric rolling workspace Pinning freezes which flights count as normal for a metric, so new flights are compared with those flights instead of with everything flown so far. Pin from a Trends panel; unpin here or there. Stratification fixed — Temperatures and EGT are compared with flights flown in similar outside air temperature, and cruise fuel figures with flights at similar density altitude, so weather is not mistaken for an engine change. The bands are shown for information. Models — workspace The takeoff-boost model's fit (R², number of takeoffs, scatter) and a Refit button.

docs.title: Settings → Engine
docs.text: Setting Default Scope What it does Engine profile chosen at workspace creation workspace Which Operators Manual the limits come from. Cannot be changed afterwards; make a new workspace. OM limits per engine read-only The full table; see Operators Manual limits by engine. The Suppression column says when a limit is checked — only in some flight phases, or only once it has been exceeded for a set time — so expected moments such as takeoff power are not reported as exceedances. Engine overrides none read-only None means every limit is the Operators Manual value shown; nothing has been changed for this aircraft. Log channels not assigned workspace What a general-purpose input carries depends on how your aircraft's EIS is configured, so the app never guesses — an unassigned channel stays viewable under its raw name. Assigning one (for example CO ppm) is recorded in the Journal and triggers re-analysis.

docs.title: Topic card → Edit rules…
docs.text:
Setting Default Scope What it does enabled on workspace Stops this topic reporting on every flight; past Journal entries stay. The card remains, collapsed, with Enable. n_min 10 workspace As above, per trigger. r2_min (trend triggers) 0.5 workspace How clearly the points must line up before a trend is reported — lower reports trends sooner, with more false alarms. z (boost-at-takeoff threshold) 2.0 workspace How far from your own boost model a takeoff must sit, in multiples of your usual scatter, before it is flagged. severity per trigger workspace The label an insight carries. Display only. Preview counts — — Counts flights, not insights: newly flagged flights gain an insight from this topic, cleared ones lose it, and changed ones keep it at a different severity.

Triggers that follow an Operators Manual limit are shown as such and have no number to edit.

docs.text: Setting Default Scope What it does Units Imperial app °F / psi / inHg / gal, or °C / bar / hPa / L. Changes display only. Workspace that reopens on launch last used app Share a workspace — Include logs / Anonymise logs on / off — See Sharing a workspace. Storage — app Shown when the app runs in your browser. Space used by each workspace; whether the browser has agreed to keep the data (if not, export a copy to be safe); Export all workspaces…; Delete all data on this device. Logs are never stored here. Make your own from the chart's Save as preset…; rename, reorder, duplicate or delete here.

docs.title: Journal
docs.text: Item What it means Live effect What this decision is doing to your flights right now — events hidden, insights added or removed, verdicts changed — recounted from your current analyses each time the Journal opens. Change notices A decision whose basis has moved since you made it — for example, a limit filter whose recent flights now breach or drift from its band, or one that no longer changes anything — so you can check it still holds.

docs.title: Flight view header
docs.text: Item What it means Excluded from reference This flight is still analysed, but it no longer shapes what normal looks like for your other flights.

docs.text:
These are part of how the app works and are not settings:

Value What 10 min Minimum airborne time for a log to count as a flight. 5 min Longest gap inside a log before it is treated as corrupt. 30 s How long a reading must stay back inside a limit before an event ends. 3 s Shortest engine-computer alert that counts as more than a blip. 20 flights How many recent flights a new filter freezes as its reference. 25 h / 50 h Engine hours before a WARNING / CAUTION filter says Review due. OAT bands cold < 5 °C · mild 5–20 °C · warm 20–30 °C · hot > 30 °C DA bands low < 2,000 ft · moderate 2,000–5,000 · high 5,000–9,000 · very high > 9,000

docs.title: Export and import
docs.text: Five minutes. How to hand your whole workspace — flights, decisions and all — to another pilot, your mechanic, or anyone helping you read your engine; and how to open one someone sent you. The same export is your backup: the workspace lives in your browser's storage, and an export is the only copy that survives the site's data being cleared. Make one after each batch of decisions.

docs.title: 1. Decide what to share
docs.text:
Open Settings → App → Share a workspace. Two choices:

  • Include logs — on by default. The logs are what the recipient's app analyses; without them they get a description of a workspace but nothing to look at. Leave this on unless the recipient already has the logs.
  • Anonymise logs — off by default. Replaces your tail number and avionics ID with a pseudonym, blanks the GPS track and radio columns, and renames the files. Dates, times and engine hours stay, because the analysis needs them. The notice under the checkboxes says exactly this, every time.

The export is always the whole active workspace. To share only some flights, make a workspace that points at a folder containing just those logs, and export that.

Settings → App: include logs, anonymise, export, import.

docs.title: 2. Check your own words
docs.text: If you chose to anonymise, the export dialog lists the places where your tail number still appears in text you typed — notes, filter reasons, the workspace name. The app does not rewrite your words; edit them first if it matters.

docs.title: 3. Export
docs.text: Export workspace… writes one file: a .zip when logs are included, a small .eisworkspace file when not. Send it however you like. It contains your settings, every decision in force (filters, rule edits, exclusions, pins), your Journal and annotations, and the list of your flights — not the analysis results, which the recipient's app recomputes, and nothing about your computer or folder paths.

docs.title: 1. Open the file
docs.text: Settings → App → Import workspace…, or Import workspace… from the workspace switcher in the top bar. Import always creates a new workspace; it never changes one you have.

docs.title: 2. Read the summary
docs.text: Before anything is created, the app shows what is in the file: whose it is, which engine and app version, how many flights, how many filters and rule edits. The new workspace's name defaults to the sender's with (imported) added. If the file came from a newer version of the app than yours, the import is refused with a message; from an older one it proceeds with a notice.

docs.title: 3. Let it match the logs
docs.text:
The logs are unpacked into a folder of their own and matched against the sender's flight list:

38 of 40 flights found · 2 missing · 12 other logs held out

Then the usual analysis runs. You see the workspace as the sender saw it — their filters, exclusions and pins in force, their Journal entries, their annotations.

docs.title: 4. Understand the leftovers
docs.text:
• A flight the sender had but whose log did not arrive is listed under Skipped as In the sender's workspace — log not found. The sender's decisions about it wait until the log appears.
  • A log that was in the zip but not in the sender's workspace — perhaps they had skipped it — is held out, listed with Include if you want it.

docs.title: A note on what you are sharing
docs.text: An engine log carries your tail number, your avionics' serial number, the date and time of every flight and your GPS track. Anonymising removes the identity and the track. The dates remain. If that is more than you want to share, share fewer flights. See Sharing a workspace.

docs.title: Reading your first flight
docs.text: Five minutes. Open any flight from the Flights page — a longer one with a proper cruise is the most informative.

docs.title: The header: facts, not judgements
docs.text:
The top line is the date, duration, engine hours and the airport the log was named after. Beneath it, Flight facts: fuel burned, cruise miles per gallon, cruise fuel flow, and whether the lane check covered both lanes. These are logbook numbers for your planning. They are never compared with anything and never raise an alert, because wind, weight and the power you chose dominate them.

Contributes to reference means this flight is part of what the app considers normal for your engine.

Header with flight facts, this flight's insights, and the timeline with its phases.

docs.title: The left column: what needs your attention
docs.text:
Insights lists anything the app found worth saying about this flight. A LIMIT badge means an Operators Manual limit was crossed; the line under it says which, how far and for how long. A WATCH badge means a reading was unusual for your engine, or a trend has become clear. If the column is empty, nothing was flagged — the flight was ordinary.

Each insight offers the next step: View evidence jumps the chart to the moment; Filter this limit… and Edit trigger are decisions, covered in the next walkthrough.

docs.title: The timeline: the flight as the engine saw it
docs.text:
The chart plots a handful of channels — the Overview preset shows RPM, airspeed, oil temperature and EGT spread — each scaled to its own range so that shapes line up. Real values with units appear at the cursor. The coloured bands behind the traces are the phases of flight, and the caption below lists how long each lasted. Switch presets (Cylinders, Thermal, Power, Fuel system, Electrical) or add a channel to see something else; zoom with − and +.

Phases as coloured bands; durations in the caption.

docs.title: The Events table: limits and alerts
docs.text:
Below the chart, every Operators Manual limit crossed on this flight, and every unexpected engine-computer alert, as one row each: the time, the phase, which limit, how long, by how much. Chart jumps to the moment. A row is a fact about the flight; what to do about it is yours to decide.

Two limits exceeded on this flight, listed with duration and excess.

docs.title: The Analysis section: one card per topic
docs.text:
Each topic the app watches has a card. Most are collapsed to one line — this flight's number, your usual, the manual's limit:

Oil temperature peak · Peak 206°F. Your average: 200°F ± 12°F (47 flights). OM limit: 248°F.

Read across the line and you have the whole picture for that topic. A card expands only when it has something to add. The ? on each card explains what the topic measures and what a change can point to.

Cards with nothing to add stay on one line.

docs.title: Two notes you will see early on
docs.text:
Still building your reference — N more flights means there is not yet enough history to compare against; the number is shown, the judgement is withheld.

Not yet validated on this engine appears on a 915iS or 912iS: the topic works, but no data from such an engine has yet confirmed it behaves sensibly there.

docs.title: Reading habit
docs.text:
One unusual flight is a note to yourself. The same thing unusual on several flights is a pattern, and the place to see patterns is Trends, which is what the concept pages Your reference and Trends are about.

Next: From an insight to a decision.

docs.title: Open the app and your first workspace
docs.text: About fifteen minutes, most of it the app working. You need a computer with a current browser — the app is tested on macOS Chrome and Safari — and a folder of engine logs from your Garmin G3X, Garmin Pilot or AXIS. Nothing to install.

docs.title: 1. Open the app
docs.text:
Open SlingologyEIS in your browser. The first time, the page sets up the analysis engine — about 30 MB, downloaded once and kept by your browser — and shows its progress. Later visits take a few seconds, and work without a network: the app starts from the copy your browser kept. When a new version is published, the next visit with a network picks it up and says Updated to version … once.

Everything the app does from here on happens inside your browser, on your computer. Your logs are read from your own folders and never uploaded; the results are kept by your browser, on this device. There is no account and no server holding your data.

Prefer to run it yourself?

The same app can run as a small program on your own computer instead, with the workspace kept in an ordinary folder. See Running the app on your own computer at the end of this page. Everything else in this guide is the same either way.

docs.title: 2. Create a workspace
docs.text:
The app asks for a workspace name and the engine model, with an optional tail number. Name it after the aircraft. Choose the engine carefully — it decides which Operators Manual limits apply and cannot be changed later (you would make a new workspace).

Your new workspace, before any logs.

docs.title: 3. Point it at your logs
docs.text:
No logs yet?

Skip this step and the next: download the sample workspace (10 MB) and use Settings → App → Import workspace… instead. It is a season of flights from the aircraft the app was developed on, decisions included. Pick up again at step 5 — the sample has four ground runs in Skipped, and the export and import walkthrough explains what an import does.

Click Choose folder… and pick the folder where you keep your logs — subfolders are included. Or drop files onto the page. The app only reads this folder; it never copies, moves or renames anything in it. You can add more folders later, and if you move logs around, Sync finds them again.

How the browser remembers the folder differs:

  • Chrome keeps the folder from one visit to the next. Now and then it asks you to confirm — the folder row shows Allow access; one click and you are back.
  • Safari does not keep folder access between visits. Your flights and analyses are all still there; the folder row says Not connected — reconnect, and you pick the folder again only when you want to sync new logs or open a flight's charts. The app says this once, on the row, the first time.

The app lists everything it found with Needs analysis beside each log, and an Analyze N button appears.

docs.title: 4. Analyze
docs.text:
Click Analyze. The app reads each log, decides whether it is a flight, works out the phases of flight, checks the Operators Manual limits and builds your reference. A season of logs takes a minute or two; the page shows progress per log. Leave the tab open until it finishes — the browser warns you if you try to close it mid-way.

When it finishes, a notice sums up what happened — 58 new flights analyzed · 59 skipped — not a flight — and the list fills in.

Every flight with its date, duration, engine hours, insights and source file.

This workspace lives in your browser

Clearing the site's data would remove it. Before you go further, see step 7, Keep a copy — an export takes a few seconds.

docs.title: 5. Look at what was skipped
docs.text:
Click Skipped. Logs that did not become flights are listed with the reason: a ground run, a flight under ten minutes, a log with a gap in it. This is normal — every engine start writes a log, and most of a year's logs are not flights. If one looks wrong, open it to check and click Include.

Skipped logs, each with its reason, each includable.

docs.title: 6. What to expect from the first flights
docs.text: Your reference needs about ten flights before it can say what is usual for your engine. Until then, cards show their numbers with still building instead of a comparison, and the Trends page says building reference. The Operators Manual checks work from the first flight.

docs.title: 7. Keep a copy
docs.text:
Your workspace lives in your browser's storage for this site. That survives closing the tab, restarting the browser and app updates — but it is gone if you clear the site's data, and a browser short of disk space — or Safari, after a long time without a visit — may clear it on its own. Settings → App → Storage shows how much space the app uses and whether the browser has agreed to keep it. Export workspace… on the same page writes a single file that restores everything; make one once your first analysis is done, and again after you have made decisions you would not want to redo. The export and import walkthrough has the details.

Next: Reading your first flight. To understand what just happened, Logs, flights and workspaces.

docs.title: Running the app on your own computer
docs.text:
The app can also run as a small program on your Mac, Windows or Linux computer, with the workspace kept in an ordinary folder (~/SlingologyEIS) rather than in the browser. Pilots choose this when they want the data in a folder they can back up like any other, when several browsers on one machine should share one workspace, or when they add log folders by typing a path. The screens, the analysis and the results are identical.

You need Python 3.10 or later. Download the latest slingology_eis…whl file from the project's releases page, then in a terminal:

pip install slingology_eis-<version>-py3-none-any.whl
slingology-eis serve

The last line prints an address — http://127.0.0.1:8420/ — open it in your browser. Leave the terminal window open while you use the app; Ctrl-C there stops it. Nothing listens on your network; the app is reachable only from this computer.

The differences you will notice: log folders are added by typing their path (or dropping files) and stay connected without any browser permissions; Settings → App shows Data location instead of Storage; and the workspace is in that folder, so the browser's site data does not matter. A workspace export from one way of running the app imports into the other.

docs.title: From an insight to a decision
docs.text: Ten minutes. This follows one real case: a fuel-pressure limit that is exceeded on most flights because of the installation, and what to do about it so it stops burying everything else.

docs.title: 1. Notice the pattern
docs.text:
On the Flights page, nearly every flight carries a LIMIT badge. Open one and the insight reads:

⚠ [CAUTION] Fuel pressure maximum: 3 events, worst 49.3 psi (max 46.0 psi), 11 min 36 s past the limit.

The insights column: a takeoff-RPM overshoot and a fuel-pressure excursion.

A limit crossed once is worth a look. A limit crossed on 48 of 58 flights by about the same margin is a characteristic of this aircraft, and the question becomes: do I understand it, and do I accept it? In this case the fuel-pressure sender reads a few psi high, confirmed against a gauge at the annual. That is a reason — and the app wants the reason written down.

docs.title: 2. Open the filter editor
docs.text:
Click Filter this limit… on the insight (or on the event's row in the Events table). The editor opens in place and starts by telling you what it knows:

On the 48 of your flights that went past this limit, it typically went 3.3 psi past, at most 4.6 psi.

The filter editor: magnitude, duration, phases, and the reason.

docs.title: 3. Choose what to tolerate
docs.text:
Three conditions, any one of which tolerates an event:

  • A little past the limit is fine, up to — the app suggests the worst you have seen, 4.6 psi, which with the 46 psi limit means readings up to 50.6 psi. Set it to what you actually accept.
  • Brief events are fine, lasting up to — leave unticked here; duration is not the issue.
  • Events in these phases are fine — leave unticked; this excursion happens in cruise, where it matters most.

Write the reason in Why is this fine on your aircraft? It appears in the Journal and in any export you share.

docs.title: 4. Preview, then apply
docs.text:
Click Preview. The app counts the effect across the whole workspace before anything changes:

This would hide 175 events on 48 of 58 flights; no flight would show a breach.

That last part is the check that the band is wide enough for the pattern you know, and no wider. Then Apply to all flights — and note the caption above it: All flights in this workspace — this limit. A filter is a statement about your aircraft, not about one flight.

docs.title: 5. What changes
docs.text:
On every Flight view, those fuel-pressure events collapse into one line — N events within your filter, up to +4.6 psi — expandable if you want them. The LIMIT badges those flights carried only for this reason disappear from the Flights page, and the insights that remain are the ones that are new.

The same flight afterwards: the fuel-pressure events are within your filter, labelled INFO.

What does not change: the Operators Manual limit still reads 46 psi, the events are still detected and still appear on the Trends page's Limit: fuel press max panel, and the app has frozen a reference of your twenty most recent flights with this event.

docs.title: 6. What the app keeps watching
docs.text:
Open the Journal. The filter is listed with its status — Stable to begin with — and a live count of what it is doing. From now on every new flight is compared with the frozen reference. If the sender starts reading five psi high instead of three, or events become more frequent, the status changes to Drifting; an event the band does not cover shows as a Breach; after 50 engine hours it asks for a Review. Each of these is counted on the Journal badge in the top bar and announced in a banner on the Flights page, so a filter never becomes a blind spot.

Journal → Limit filters: status, how far past the limit each flight went, time past the limit, and the frozen reference.

docs.title: The other decisions
docs.text:
The same shape — see the effect, state the scope, record it in the Journal — applies to the rest:

  • Edit trigger on an insight, or Edit rules… on any topic card, opens the rule editor beside the card. Change how many flights a comparison needs or how strong a trend must be; a live preview counts how many flights would gain or lose an insight; Apply to all flights.
  • Exclude this flight from reference on an insight, or the flight's header: give a reason and the flight stops shaping what others are compared against. This flight only.
  • Enable/disable a topic in the rule editor: the card stays on every flight, collapsed, with Enable.

All of them are explained on Your decisions. Next: Export and import.
